verdict.rationale: The proclamation and teaching of the word is commanded as central to the gathered people of God across the whole canon. In 2 Timothy 4:2 keryxon ton logon (G2784 aorist imperative governing G3056) is a direct command to preach the word, Romans 10:14 to 17 makes faith arise ex akoes dia rhematos, by hearing through the word, and Acts 2:42 reports the first community devoting itself to the apostles' didache (G1322). The same vocabulary fills the Old Testament, with dabar (H1697, 1368 occurrences), the public reading of the torah to the assembled people in Deuteronomy 31:11 to 12 and Nehemiah 8:8, and the prophet commanded to speak God's word faithfully in Jeremiah 23:28. Confidence is medium not because the centrality of the word is weak, but because no verse pairs ekklesia (G1577) with any sign or mark term (G4592 semeion never co-occurs with G1577), so the specific framing of preaching as a formal note distinguishing a true church from a false one is a synthesis the vocabulary supports in substance but does not itself enumerate.

scripture.force: The verse opens with keryxon ton logon, where keryxon is the aorist active imperative second singular of kerysso (G2784=V-AAM-2S) and logon is its accusative direct object (G3056=N-ASM). This is a direct command to preach the word, followed by reprove, rebuke, and exhort in all patience and didache (G1322). The grammar gives the strongest possible form of the obligation: not a description of what some did, but an imperative laid on the one who serves the assembly. The clustering of preaching, teaching, and exhortation in a single charge makes the ministry of the word the named duty.

The chain of Romans 10:14 to 17 runs from calling to believing to hearing to a preacher, where the one preaching is kerysso as a present active participle (G2784=V-PAP-GSM) and the act of preaching is an aorist subjunctive (G2784=V-AAS-3P) conditioned on being sent. Verse 17 concludes ara he pistis ex akoes, he de akoe dia rhematos, faith comes from hearing and hearing through the word (G4487=N-GSN). The grammar makes the preached word the necessary cause of faith, so a community in which the word is not proclaimed cannot generate the faith that constitutes it.

The gathered believers were continually devoting themselves to the didache of the apostles, listed first among the habitual devotions of the new community alongside fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayers. The apostolic teaching heads the list and is described as a sustained activity, presenting the taught word as a constitutive practice of the assembled church rather than an optional supplement.

Timothy is told to devote himself to the public reading (anagnosis), to exhortation (paraklesis, G3874), and to teaching (didaskalia, G1319), three datives governed by the imperative prosechе. These are named as the standing public activities the minister owes the church until Christ comes. The triad of reading, exhortation, and teaching describes the verbal ministry of the word as the ordered work of the assembly's leadership.

The elder must hold fast the faithful word that accords with the teaching, tou kata ten didachen pistou logou, so that he is able both to exhort in sound didaskalia (G1319) and to refute those who contradict. Right teaching is written into the qualification for the very officers who order a church, so the appointment of leadership in Titus 1:5 is tied directly to fidelity in the word here in verse 9.

The church of the living God is called the pillar (stylos) and support (hedraioma) of the aletheia (G0225). The building metaphor casts the assembly's defining function as upholding and displaying the truth, which presupposes that truth is being declared and taught within it. This is the closest the vocabulary comes to a defining role for the church, and it is stated in terms of the truth it bears, not in terms of a formal mark that sorts true from false assemblies.

This is the one verse in the canon where ekklesia (G1577=N-DSF) and logos (G3056) stand together: en ekklesia, in the assembly, Paul would rather speak five intelligible words that he might instruct others (katecheo, G2727=V-AAS-1S) than ten thousand in a tongue. The pairing ties the spoken, understood word directly to the gathered church and grounds it in the goal of instruction, which is exactly the activity the proposition names.

Israel is commanded to assemble (haqhel) the people, men, women, children, and the sojourner, that they may hear (shama, H8085) and learn (lamad) and fear the LORD and keep the words of the torah (H8451). The verse joins the gathered assembly directly to the public hearing and learning of God's word, showing the same constitutive role for the word among the Old Testament people as the New Testament gives the church.

The prophet who has God's word is commanded to speak that word faithfully, yedabber debari emeth, let him speak my word in truth, set against the one who tells his own dream. The verse fixes faithfulness of the spoken word (dabar, H1697) as the standard for the true messenger, the Old Testament counterpart to the New Testament charge to preach the word, which is why the cross-reference apparatus links it to Romans 10:17 on the keyword of hearing.

Christ promises to be present where two or three gather in his name. Read alone the verse could be taken to make bare gathering sufficient for a true assembly apart from any proclamation, but its setting is church discipline grounded in the binding and loosing of verses 18 and 19, which presupposes a community acting on a declared standard. The verse therefore does not displace the word but assumes it, so it is treated here as a text that does not directly weigh either way.

complicating_texts.resolution: The promise that Christ is present where two or three gather in his name could be read to make mere gathering, apart from any proclamation, sufficient for a true assembly. Its immediate context is church discipline grounded in the binding and loosing of verses 18 and 19, which presupposes a community acting on a declared standard, so the verse assumes rather than replaces the role of the word.

The verse lists didache alongside fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer, which could suggest teaching is only one of four parallel and equally optional items. The four are presented as habitual devotions that together describe the church, and didache heads the list, so the data supports teaching as constitutive rather than dispensable.

This verse comes closest to a defining role for the church by calling it the pillar and support of the truth, but it states that role in terms of the truth the church upholds, not in terms of a sign or mark that distinguishes a true church from a false one. The lexical search found no verse anywhere in the canon that pairs ekklesia (G1577) with a sign or mark term (G4592 semeion), so the specific notae ecclesiae framing in the proposition cannot be resolved to a stated lexical category. It is left unaddressed at the level of the words because the vocabulary supports the substance but does not supply the formal mark concept.

variants.note: The cited verses fall outside the open-cbgm 3 John sample, so CBGM data was not examined and ecm_status is shadow rather than published. The apparatus marks present in the bundle at Acts 2:42, Matthew 28:19 to 20, Matthew 18:15 to 19, Romans 10:14 to 15, and Titus 1:5 concern word order and minor readings that do not touch the lexemes for preaching, word, teaching, or church, so they do not move the verdict.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reading the proposition as the claim that preaching and teaching the word is a central, commanded, constitutive activity of a true assembly yields direct and strong support. The imperative keryxon ton logon in 2 Timothy 4:2, the faith from hearing of Romans 10:17, the apostolic didache of Acts 2:42, the reading, exhortation, and teaching triad of 1 Timothy 4:13, and the public reading of the torah in Deuteronomy 31:12 and Nehemiah 8:8 converge on the word as the indispensable verbal ministry of the gathered people.

Reading the proposition strictly as asserting a formal note or sign that distinguishes a true visible church from a false one finds the underlying substance in the texts but no lexeme that erects the mark as a juridical test. No verse pairs ekklesia with a sign or mark word, so on this reading the proposition is an inference drawn from the constitutive data rather than a stated category, which a reader holding to a strict marks taxonomy should recognize as a synthesis above the word level.

A reader who weights Matthew 18:20 most heavily could argue that the presence of Christ among two or three gathered in his name is what makes an assembly real, with the word important but not erected as a defining mark. Stated in its strongest form this reading is honest about the verse, but the surrounding discipline context and the canon-wide insistence that faith comes by the heard word mean the gathering it describes already presupposes a declared standard rather than dispensing with proclamation.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict rests on the convergence of many texts across both Testaments (analogia scripturae): the preaching imperative of 2 Timothy 4:2, the faith from hearing of Romans 10:14 to 17, the apostolic teaching of Acts 2:42, the verbal ministry triad of 1 Timothy 4:13, the elder qualification of Titus 1:9, the pillar of truth identity of 1 Timothy 3:15, the word in the assembly of 1 Corinthians 14:19, and the Old Testament public reading and prophetic faithfulness of Deuteronomy 31:12, Nehemiah 8:8, and Jeremiah 23:28. Progressive revelation is in play because the Old Testament reading of the torah to the assembly is fulfilled and intensified in the New Testament command to preach the word, the same pattern carried forward.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: The proclamation, reading, and teaching of God's word is presented in the cited texts as a central and commanded activity of the gathered people of God.
stem_audit.notes: The phrase mark of a true visible church imports a formal notae ecclesiae taxonomy that frames the claim as a distinguishing test between true and false churches. A direct lexical search confirmed that no verse in the canon pairs ekklesia (G1577) with any sign or mark term (G4592 semeion), so the mark versus counterfeit framing is a confessional synthesis that no single lexeme supplies. The lexical data strongly supports the underlying claim that the proclaimed and taught word is central and constitutive to the assembly, so the verdict on the original stem is affirms at medium confidence: the substance is lexically secure, the formal mark category is an inference held with caution. The verdict was derived on the original stem.

lay_summary: The verses behind this proposition tie the gathered church tightly to the preaching, reading, and teaching of God's word, and the pattern runs through the whole Bible. In Second Timothy 4:2 the very first words are a direct command, preach the word, where the verb is an imperative and the word is its object, followed at once by reprove, rebuke, exhort, and teach. Romans 10:14 to 17 builds a chain from calling to believing to hearing to a sent preacher and ends by saying faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word, so where the word is not proclaimed the faith that makes a church cannot arise. Acts 2:42 reports the first believers continually devoting themselves to the apostles' teaching, named first among their habitual practices. First Timothy 4:13 tells the minister to give himself to the public reading, to exhortation, and to teaching, and Titus 1:9 requires an elder to hold the faithful word so he can teach and refute. The same vocabulary fills the Old Testament. The word of God, the verb to hear, the act of proclaiming or reading aloud, and the instruction of the law all occur thousands of times, the people are gathered in Deuteronomy and Nehemiah to hear the law read so they can understand and obey, and Jeremiah commands the prophet who has God's word to speak it faithfully. Taken together the words make the spoken and taught word a central, commanded activity of a real assembly, not an optional feature. One point keeps the confidence at medium. A direct search of the text found that no verse anywhere pairs the word for church with any word for sign or mark. So the strong substance, that the word is central and constitutive, is plainly in the text, but the further idea of calling this a formal mark that sorts a true church from a false one is a summary drawn from the texts rather than something any single word states, and that part is held with more caution while the underlying claim stands firmly on the lexical evidence.
